# Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX — facts

## Structure and components

- [statement] Harbor’s navigation-state discussion contains conflicting positions: the reporter wants page and search criteria restored on Back; one contributor defends refreshing on re-entry and suggests opening details in another tab; another proposes restoring criteria from the URL while fetching results again. The latter is a proposal, not evidence of an implemented fix. (low confidence) — https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/issues/23142 · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## How it works

- [statement] Communicate the effect of search and filtering with result counts and distinguish waiting from completion or no results. Pencil & Paper recommends counts as feedback on narrowing; W3C identifies brief search-status messages as status updates when they neither take focus nor refresh the page. W3C explicitly excludes the result list itself from that status-message definition. (medium confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html
- [statement] NN/G warns that moving the page while someone is selecting filters can make them lose their place or click the wrong control. It also notes that keeping the old scroll position can hide a short result list and resemble an unfinished or empty search. Decide when to reveal updated results in relation to the user’s current filtering activity. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Hearst’s search-interface evaluation chapter recommends realistic tasks and comparisons over the same document collection. It cautions that prewritten queries reduce realism for query-formulation research, although they can be acceptable when evaluating result-summary assessment. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Filter application should account for intent, selection complexity and response speed. NN/G recommends interactive updates for exploration and batch application for known multi-criterion searches or slow responses; Pencil & Paper likewise distinguishes instant, per-filter and global application. Neither supports one application mode for every search task. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering
- [statement] Hearst’s search-interface evaluation guidance recommends realistic tasks and considers time, effort and error severity. It cautions that longer exploration can reflect a better experience, so shorter sessions alone do not establish success. Prewritten query terms can isolate result-summary assessment but reduce realism when evaluating query formulation or term suggestions. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Immediate filtering is conditional on the task and response speed. NN/g recommends interactive updates for exploration and batch application for known compound criteria or slow responses; Pencil & Paper likewise recommends a global Apply action for heavy datasets or slow applications. These are design recommendations, not a measured universal performance advantage. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX · also: https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering
- [statement] Hearst identifies task time, effort and error severity as interface evaluation measures but cautions against equating shorter sessions with better search: longer exploration and refinement can be useful. Search evaluation should interpret timing in the context of the task and participant differences. (low confidence) — https://searchuserinterfaces.com/book/sui_ch2_evaluation.html · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In Baymard’s desktop ecommerce testing, some users treated autocomplete suggestions as editable starting points. Baymard recommends copying the keyboard-highlighted suggestion into the search field so users can refine it before submission; this is a recommendation grounded in that context, rather than a universal autocomplete rule. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/copy-search-suggestion-to-search-field · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper recommends making active filters visible outside collapsed controls and providing clearing at both individual-filter and global levels. Its advanced-filter pattern lets users add or exclude conditions and choose whether results match all, one or none; products should expose the supported composition rather than leave it implicit. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] For ecommerce zero-result recovery, Baymard recommends relevant alternative categories or simplified queries rather than search tips alone. If an alternate query is automatically applied, its recommendation includes telling users that the original query had no results and that the displayed results come from the revision. Preserve that distinction when communicating relevance. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] NN/g identifies a trade-off in batch filtering: waiting until criteria are complete avoids repeated waits, but delays feedback about available combinations and can allow a combination that produces no results. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/applying-filters/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper describes advanced filtering as composing conditions with explicit relations, including equality, ranges and and/or combinations. This guidance supports exposing compound filter logic rather than leaving users to infer how selections combine. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Baymard observed that minor misspellings could remove autocomplete guidance or produce irrelevant suggestions. Correcting spelling only after submission misses users who keep revising in the field or abandon search before submitting; evaluate typo recovery during query entry as well as on the results page. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/offer-autocomplete-suggestions-for-misspellings · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] W3C’s status-message criterion requires displayed status messages to be programmatically determinable so assistive technology can present them without receiving focus. Its guidance cautions against overly chatty announcements and does not require authors to invent additional status messages; test the feedback level with users. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] A Harbor issue records a disagreement about list navigation. The reporter says Back resets page and query; commenter AllForNothing defends refresh as protection against stale repository data. Commenter DuttaNeel07 proposes preserving page and query in the URL while fetching fresh data, with fallback if the saved page disappears. These are attributed reports and proposals, not proof of a shipped fix or current behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/issues/23142 · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Keep evidence about AI answers separate from classic result-list search. In NN/G’s exploratory remote study, traditional search and AI chat were used together and sometimes to check each other; nobody relied entirely on generated answers. The study involved nine participants from North America and the UK, so these observations do not establish population prevalence or a universal AI-search replacement effect. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-changing-search-behaviors/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard recommends retaining the submitted query in an editable search field: its ecommerce tests found that persistence lets users add or remove words without retyping the full query. It also recommends showing the query on the results page to make the origin of the results clear. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/persist-search-queries · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper describes per-filter application as an intermediate option: users finish searching and selecting within a multi-select dropdown, then apply that filter by closing the dropdown or using its inline Apply action. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Pencil & Paper recommends showing active selections in their controls, marking controls containing selections, and providing an applied-filter summary. It recommends clearing selections both within an individual filter and globally. (low confidence) — https://www.pencilandpaper.io/articles/ux-pattern-analysis-enterprise-filtering · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] The W3C explanation of the status-messages criterion distinguishes a search result list from messages about its progress or completion. Search progress, result-count and no-result messages that update without focus or page refresh should be programmatically available to assistive technology; the result list itself is outside this particular criterion. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard’s ecommerce research says generic search tips alone often leave users stuck. It recommends actionable related-query suggestions, including broadening an overly specific query by removing keywords, to give users a path out of zero results. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] Baymard recommends that if a zero-results search has only one alternate query, it may be applied automatically with an explicit notice that the original query returned nothing and the displayed results come from the revised search. This is attributed ecommerce guidance, not a universal rule for exact-match or high-stakes search. (low confidence) — https://baymard.com/research-articles/no-results-page · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
- [statement] NN/g’s qualitative study used remote usability sessions with nine participants from North America and the UK. All used traditional search multiple times and none relied entirely on generative responses. This finding concerns those sessions; it does not establish population adoption rates or prove that AI answers replace result-list interaction. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-changing-search-behaviors/ · keywords: Search query, result-state and filter interaction UX
